title: Mira and the Quiet Quill
markdown:
Willow Creek Library had been polished until the oak shelves smelled of beeswax and the tea urn kept a thin silver note. Tonight was Ancient Artifacts evening, maps of vanished coasts hung like quiet flags, and Mira the fox, spectacles slipping the familiar millimetre down her muzzle, had brought a quill. It had belonged to a clerk of only moderate fame, a person whose letters survived because Mira had spent winter evenings coaxing ink-rot from the shaft and setting the barb so it would not split. She did not expect a prize. She hoped, privately, that someone might notice the work.

Bea the goat, her flatmate, was assisting by sorting bookmarks into colour gradients that made no catalogue sense. The process involved contented chewing and the occasional bleat of scholarly satisfaction.

“Are you quite certain about this, Bea?” Mira asked. She was watching the evening’s programmes, which had been tied with a red ribbon of independent character. The ribbon kept unfurling. The librarian’s neat stack became a small rebellion of paper.

“A little disarray keeps the blood moving,” Bea said, muffled by cardstock. “And that quill of yours looks bristly with history. As if it has been waiting to be asked a decent question.”

The air was aged paper, polish, and tea. Visitors had not yet arrived, but the room already felt crowded with other centuries. Mira’s flutter, which had been almost pleasant, grew less so when Horace the goose filled the doorway as if it had been measured for him. His honk was a low rumble of committee. He surveyed the labels, found them wanting, and began tapping corrections with his beak, a tiny percussion of academic rectitude.

“Good evening, Mira.” He did not look at her. “I trust we are observing the appropriate rigor. This misplaced comma, for instance—” a wing toward Discover the Secrets of the Pyramids!—“is a blemish upon historical discourse.”

Mira felt the old smallness, the cub-footed sense that she had arrived with jam on her paws. Horace did not attend evenings. He annexed them. He moved through the displays as though history were a speech he had already given, and the objects were merely his notes.

Later, among a tray of Roman coins worn to the colour of river stones, Bea trotted up with an apple, slightly gnawed and still perfectly good.

“You look as if you have swallowed a pebble,” Bea said.

“It is Horace.” Mira’s shoulders folded. “He is so certain. Everyone listens as if certainty were conservation. My quill feels like a footnote he would strike.”

Bea bit the apple, then offered Mira the rest, a flick of the head that was somehow both rude and kind. “It is not a footnote. It is quiet. Quiet is not the same as small. Horace is busy announcing what things ought to mean. You keep the things that mean them. The work that does not make a fuss is still work.”

Mira took the apple. Juice, ordinary and sharp. She did not argue. Somewhere behind her Horace honked at a date that had dared to be approximate.

When the doors opened, townsfolk and two visiting historians filled the aisle with their careful shoes. Horace held court by the papyrus, a torrent of fibre counts and humidity. Mira found other conversations, the unhurried kind that do not require a lectern. An elderly gentleman turned a coin in his fingers and remembered a biscuit tin, a rainy afternoon, a child’s certainty that Rome had been a place you could walk to if you followed the right hedge. A girl stood a long time at the quill. She did not ask for the owner’s rank. She asked whether the writer had paused, sometimes, between sentences, and whether the pause had been part of the letter too.

Mira looked at the red ribbon, still refusing the stack. She looked at Horace’s improved comma, which had not improved the pyramids. Then she did one small thing she had not planned. She turned the quill in the lamplight until the nib caught, and she left it there, unlabeled by anyone’s grammar.

The girl leaned in. The gentleman smiled without announcing that he had smiled. Mira answered the questions she actually knew: how the barb had been mended, how beeswax kept the shaft from thirst, how a quiet tool could outlast a loud reputation. Curiosity did the rest. It did not need a honk.

Closing came gently. The programmes remained slightly untidy. Horace, to a dedicated audience of three polite chairs, had moved on to Bronze Age temper. Mira packed the coins first, each into its felt. The quill went last, in its lined box, the nib still holding a little of the lamp. On the table the red ribbon lay where it had chosen to lie, a bright uncorrected curl. Bea bleated once, softly, as if to say that was enough of a review, and the library kept its other centuries to itself.
